episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. We’re also on video! Check us out on YouTube. Subscribe to The Verge for unlimited access to theverge.com, subscriber-exclusive newsletters, and our ad-free podcast feed. We love hearing from you! transcript_window.text: So the thing that they do is they get 100 kits of stuff, a bunch of cables and nonsense inside of suitcases, and they put them in people's houses and they just ask them to use them.
Did George tell you about this early testing process?
Yeah, key thing about any technology is you need to have a reason for it to exist, right?
You need a use case.
You shouldn't really be working from the technology towards the use case, but find the use cases and solve the problem.
Obviously, they were doing it the wrong way around, but they found a lot of use cases straight away.
But you know what's interesting about that?
They didn't find one.
Do you know what I mean?
I think a lot of times you go on a process like this and you find, like the Amazon Echo is a good version of this, right?
They went out and found, use this to listen to music.
This is fundamentally a sort of universally music -based product.
And then everybody has little things that they want to do on the side so we can build a whole ecosystem.
But from everything I found in the research, one of the weirdest things about smart lighting was that everybody immediately found use cases for it and none of them were the same.
I actually ended up setting up a routine where my light would turn red if my boss had emailed me.
Why?
was super helpful.
You wake up at one o 'clock in the morning and all your lights are red and you're like, oh God.
has happened?
I would just have one light.
Not all of them.
But yeah, that would have been kind of terrifying.
I can imagine.
And Nilay would like love that.
The power.
Oh, yeah.
